learn.title: Flow Batteries for Grid Storage
learn.intro: Flow batteries offer scalable, long-duration storage crucial for balancing renewable energy intermittency. Their ability to decouple power and energy capacity makes them ideal for stabilizing grids reliant on solar and wind.
learn.c1_text: VRFBs use liquid electrolytes stored in tanks, enabling unlimited energy capacity by simply increasing tank size. They’re like rechargeable power packs for the grid, with lifespans exceeding 20 years and 10,000+ charge cycles.
learn.c2_text: Iron-based systems use abundant, low-cost materials like iron and saltwater. They’re cheaper than VRFBs but less energy-dense, making them suitable for large-scale, cost-sensitive projects.
learn.c3_text: India’s grid faces 24/7 power demands, requiring storage for solar-rich regions. Flow batteries can provide 4–8 hours of backup, critical for stabilizing grids during monsoon-driven demand spikes.
learn.stat2: VRFBs can deliver 200 kW power for 4 hours (8 MWh).
learn.stat3: Iron flow batteries cost ~$30/kWh vs. $350/kWh for lithium-ion.
learn.stat4: India’s target: 15 GW energy storage by 2030.

learn.title: Solar Panel Types Compared
learn.intro: Solar panels convert sunlight into electricity, but their efficiency and cost vary. Choosing the right type impacts energy output and long-term savings.
learn.c1_text: Made from single-crystal silicon, these panels are 20–22% efficient and ideal for limited roof space. They’re like luxury cars of solar panels—high performance but pricier.
learn.c2_text: Poly panels use silicon fragments, offering 15–17% efficiency at lower costs. They’re like economy cars: practical for larger installations with ample space.
learn.c3_text: Thin-film panels (10–13% efficient) thrive in India’s hot climate, performing better in low light. They’re used in utility-scale projects like the 2.5 GW Bhadla Solar Park.
learn.stat3: Thin-film lifespan: 15–20 years vs. 25+ for crystalline panels.
learn.stat4: India’s solar parks target 30 GW capacity by 2030.

learn.title: Electric Vehicles Explained
learn.intro: EVs reduce emissions by replacing tailpipe pollution with grid-powered energy. Understanding their components demystifies their role in decarbonizing transport.
learn.c1_text: EVs use AC/DC motors (e.g., Tesla’s induction motors) for instant torque. Unlike ICE engines, they require no gears and deliver 100% efficiency at peak performance.
learn.c2_text: Regenerative braking converts kinetic energy into electricity, recapturing 10–25% of energy lost during braking. Imagine turning a spinning wheel into a mini power generator.
learn.c3_text: India’s EV charging network grew to 8,000+ stations in 2024. Policies like FAME II subsidize charging infrastructure, aiming for 30% EV penetration by 2030.
learn.stat2: EV operating cost: ₹0.8/km vs. ₹7/km for diesel cars.
learn.stat3: Charging time: 30 mins (DC fast charger) vs. 8 hours (home charger).
learn.stat4: India’s EV battery target: 50 GWh by 2030.

learn.title: Demand Response Systems
learn.intro: Demand response programs adjust energy use during peak times, reducing grid strain. They act as a virtual battery, leveraging flexibility in industrial and residential consumption.
learn.c1_text: Large consumers (e.g., factories) reduce usage during peak hours, lowering bills by 15–20%. It’s like turning off lights during a storm to prevent overload.
learn.c2_text: By shifting demand, utilities avoid firing up inefficient peaker plants. In 2023, U.S. demand response saved $5.2 billion in avoided costs.
learn.c3_text: India’s National Virtual Grid (NVG) pilot involves 100 MW demand response from industries. It aims to cut peak demand by 10% by 2025, easing grid pressure.
learn.stat4: Commercial buildings reduce load by 15% during peaks.

learn.title: Pumped Hydro Storage
learn.intro: Pumped hydro stores energy by moving water between reservoirs. As the world’s largest storage tech, it provides reliable backup for renewables.
learn.c1_text: Excess energy pumps water uphill; during demand, water flows down through turbines. It’s like a water battery, with 70–80% round-trip efficiency.
learn.c2_text: Pumped hydro accounts for 95% of global storage. The 3,600 MW Bath County facility in the U.S. can power 200,000 homes for 8 hours.
learn.c3_text: India has 150 GW potential for pumped hydro, leveraging its mountainous terrain. Projects like the 300 MW Nathpa Jhakri plant highlight its viability.
learn.stat3: Cost: $1.2 million/kW vs. $3 million/kW for batteries.
learn.stat4: India’s target: 15 GW pumped hydro by 2050.

learn.title: Rooftop Solar & Net Metering
learn.intro: Rooftop solar lets households generate power, while net metering credits them for excess energy. This policy drives decentralized renewable adoption.
learn.c1_text: Solar panels on rooftops feed electricity into the grid. Net metering credits users for surplus power, offsetting bills. A 5 kW system in Delhi can save ₹15,000/year.
learn.c2_text: India’s net metering policy allows up to 100% credit for excess generation. However, delays in payment and state-level variations hinder adoption.
learn.c3_text: Mumbai’s rooftop solar program installed 10 MW by 2023. The MNRE offers subsidies covering 40% of costs for residential systems under 3 kW.
learn.stat2: Net metering savings: ₹12,000–₹20,000/year for 5 kW systems.
learn.stat4: Rooftop solar potential: 500 GW in India.
